title: World History
description: Key peoples, places and turning points in world history: explorers and maps, medieval societies across continents, the age of encounters, revolutions, industrialisation, empires and resistance, the World Wars, decolonisation, the Cold War and globalisation — with attention to perspectives from Asia, Africa and the Americas, not only Europe.

lessons.title: Big Buildings from Long Ago
objectives: Name famous old buildings from different countries
Know they were built by many people long ago
explanation: Long ago, people built amazing things without machines like cranes or trucks. The pyramids in Egypt were built over 4,500 years ago as tombs for kings called pharaohs.
The Great Wall of China is a very long wall built and rebuilt over many centuries to protect against invaders.
Thousands of workers moved heavy stones with ropes, ramps, sledges and lots of teamwork. These buildings help us learn about how people lived.

context.text: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BCE; archaeologists have found evidence of organised workers' villages nearby.

lessons.title: Sailing Across the Sea
objectives: Describe how people travelled long ago
Know that sailors used the stars and winds
explanation: Long ago, there were no aeroplanes or cars. People walked, rode horses or camels, and sailed boats with wind in their sails.
Sailors used the stars at night and the winds to find their way. In the Indian Ocean, sailors learned to use the monsoon winds to sail between India, Arabia and Africa.
Long journeys could take months! Travellers brought back spices, cloth and stories.

context.text: Ancient Greek and Roman texts and archaeological finds show sailors used monsoon winds to cross the Arabian Sea to India by around the 1st century BCE–1st century CE.

story.text: A trader in Kerala loaded his wooden ship with black pepper. "We wait for the right wind," the captain said. When the monsoon winds blew, the sails filled and the ship raced across the sea towards Arabia. Months later, it returned with dates, perfumes and wonderful stories.

lessons.title: The Great Travellers
objectives: Describe famous travellers and their journeys
Explain why their writings are useful to historians
explanation: Ibn Battuta, from Morocco, travelled for about 30 years in the 1300s across Africa, the Middle East, India (where he served the Sultan of Delhi) and China. He described everything he saw.
Marco Polo, from Venice, travelled to China in the 1200s. Zheng He, a Chinese admiral, led huge fleets across the Indian Ocean in the early 1400s, visiting India, Arabia and East Africa.
Travellers' accounts help historians learn about places and times — though they sometimes misunderstood what they saw or exaggerated.

context.text: Ibn Battuta's Rihla and Marco Polo's Travels survive as written accounts; historians compare them with other sources to check accuracy.

vocabulary.meaning: a person who journeys to far places
a person who travels to discover new places

examples: Ibn Battuta described Delhi and the Malabar coast.

story.title: The Man Who Couldn't Stop Travelling
story.text: In 1325, a young man named Ibn Battuta left Tangier in Morocco to go on pilgrimage to Mecca. He kept going — to Persia, India, the Maldives, China and back across Africa — for nearly 30 years. When he finally returned, he told his stories to a writer, and his book still tells us about the 14th-century world.

lessons.title: Gold of Mali and Temples of Angkor
objectives: Describe medieval kingdoms in Africa, Asia and the Americas
Know history is not only about Europe
explanation: The Mali Empire in West Africa was rich from gold and salt trade. Its ruler Mansa Musa made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, giving away so much gold in Cairo that its value there fell. Timbuktu became a centre of learning.
The Khmer Empire in Cambodia built Angkor Wat in the 12th century, originally as a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu, later becoming Buddhist.
In the Americas, the Aztecs built Tenochtitlan on a lake, and the Inca built roads across the Andes and the mountain city of Machu Picchu.

context.text: Arab chroniclers recorded Mansa Musa's pilgrimage; Angkor Wat's inscriptions and architecture show its Hindu and later Buddhist use.

lessons.title: A New Sea Route to India
objectives: Describe major European voyages of the late 1400s
Explain their consequences from multiple perspectives
explanation: In the 1400s, European rulers wanted direct access to Asian spices. In 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed west hoping to reach Asia, but reached the Caribbean instead. In 1498, Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa and reached Calicut (Kozhikode) in Kerala.
For Europeans these were "discoveries", but the lands were already home to many peoples, and Indian Ocean trade routes were already busy with Arab, Indian, Chinese and African sailors.

The voyages led to European colonies, enormous wealth for Europe, and devastating consequences for Indigenous peoples of the Americas, including disease, violence and enslavement, as well as the transatlantic slave trade from Africa.

context.text: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in May 1498; diseases such as smallpox caused catastrophic population decline among Indigenous Americans after 1492.
Historians now avoid describing these voyages simply as "discovery", recognising Indigenous peoples' perspectives.

vocabulary.meaning: a long sea journey

examples: Kappad beach near Kozhikode, where da Gama landed.

story.title: Two Views from the Shore
story.text: When Vasco da Gama's ships arrived at Calicut, local merchants were used to ships from Arabia, East Africa and China. The Zamorin (ruler) received the Portuguese, but was unimpressed by their gifts. To the Portuguese, it was a historic arrival; to Calicut's traders, it was one more group of foreign ships — at first.

lessons.title: What Crossed the Ocean?
objectives: Explain the Columbian exchange
Evaluate its effects on different regions
explanation: After 1492, plants, animals, people and diseases moved between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia. Historian Alfred Crosby called this the "Columbian exchange".

From the Americas came maize, potatoes, tomatoes, chillies, cacao and tobacco. To the Americas went wheat, rice, sugarcane, horses, cattle and pigs — and diseases like smallpox, to which Indigenous people had no immunity.
The exchange transformed diets worldwide (imagine Indian food without chilli or potato!) but also caused terrible loss of life and reshaped economies through plantations and slavery.

context.text: Alfred Crosby's 1972 book "The Columbian Exchange" introduced the term; crop origins are established by botanical and archaeological evidence.

vocabulary.meaning: transfer of plants, animals and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world after 1492
the body's ability to resist a disease
a large farm growing one crop, often with forced labour
a plant grown for food or use

examples: Horses transforming life on the American plains.

lessons.title: Steam, Factories and Cities
objectives: Explain the Industrial Revolution and its effects
Connect industrialisation in Britain to colonial India
explanation: From the late 1700s, Britain began to industrialise. New machines like spinning frames and power looms, driven by water and then steam engines (improved by James Watt), made cloth much faster in factories.
People moved from farms to crowded cities to work long hours in factories, including children. Over time, workers organised for better conditions.

Industrial Britain needed raw materials and markets. Raw cotton from India and the American South (grown by enslaved people) fed British mills, while British machine-made cloth was sold back to India, hurting Indian handloom weavers.

context.text: Historical records show child labour in British factories led to reforms such as the Factory Acts in the 1830s–40s.
Historians debate why industrialisation began first in Britain, citing factors such as coal, capital from trade and empire, and institutions.

vocabulary.meaning: the shift to machine production from the late 1700s
a building where goods are made by machines
an engine powered by steam

story.title: The Child in the Mill
story.text: In 1830s England, ten-year-old Sarah worked 12 hours a day in a cotton mill, crawling under machines to tie broken threads. The cotton she touched had been grown far away. Reformers collected stories like hers, and laws slowly began to limit children's working hours.

lessons.title: Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
objectives: Describe the American, French and Haitian Revolutions
Explain how revolutionary ideas spread and their limits
explanation: In 1776, thirteen American colonies declared independence from Britain, stating that "all men are created equal" — though slavery continued and women could not vote.
In 1789, the French Revolution overthrew the monarchy's absolute power, proclaiming "liberty, equality, fraternity" and the Declaration of the Rights of Man. It also led to terror and war.

In Haiti, enslaved Africans led by Toussaint Louverture rose up and in 1804 created the first independent Black republic, abolishing slavery. These ideas later inspired Indian thinkers; "liberty, equality, fraternity" appear in India's Preamble.

context.text: Haiti declared independence on 1 January 1804; the phrase "liberty, equality and fraternity" appears in the Preamble of India's Constitution.
Historians debate the legacies of these revolutions, including the gap between ideals and practice.

vocabulary.meaning: a major, often sudden change in government or society
rule by a king or queen
a formal statement
officially end

examples: The storming of the Bastille, 14 July 1789.

story.text: Ivaan read India's Preamble: "liberty… equality… fraternity." His teacher explained these words echoed the French Revolution, while Indian leaders gave them new meaning for a diverse nation. "Ideas travel," she said, "and each people makes them their own."

lessons.title: The World at War
objectives: Explain main causes and consequences of the two World Wars
Describe India's involvement
explanation: World War I (1914–1918) grew from rivalries between European powers, alliances, militarism and imperial competition; the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand was the trigger. Over a million Indian soldiers served, many in France, the Middle East and East Africa.

World War II (1939–1945) began with Nazi Germany's invasion of Poland. It involved most of the world. The Holocaust — the Nazi genocide of six million Jews and millions of others — is one of history's greatest crimes. About 2.5 million Indians served in the British Indian Army, the largest volunteer army in history.
The wars ended with atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki (1945), the founding of the United Nations, and weakened European empires, which helped speed decolonisation.

context.text: Indian soldiers' service is commemorated at India Gate in New Delhi and war memorials abroad; Holocaust documentation includes Nazi records, survivor testimony and physical evidence from camps.
Historians weigh multiple causes of the wars differently.

story.title: Letters from the Front
story.text: During World War I, Indian soldiers in France wrote letters home describing cold trenches, snow they had never seen, and kindness from French villagers. Censors kept copies, and today historians read them to understand the soldiers' experiences — far from home, fighting in a war that was not their own.

lessons.title: A Wave of New Nations
objectives: Describe decolonisation in Asia and Africa
Explain the Non-Aligned Movement and the anti-apartheid struggle
explanation: After 1945, dozens of colonies became independent. India and Pakistan (1947) were among the first; Indonesia, Ghana (1957, led by Kwame Nkrumah), Kenya, Algeria and many others followed, some through negotiation and some through long wars.
Many new nations, led by figures including Nehru, Egypt's Nasser, Indonesia's Sukarno and Yugoslavia's Tito, formed the Non-Aligned Movement (1961), refusing to join either Cold War bloc.

In South Africa, apartheid — legal racial segregation — was resisted for decades. Nelson Mandela, imprisoned for 27 years, became president in 1994. Gandhi's early activism in South Africa inspired later movements.

context.text: Gandhi lived in South Africa from 1893 to 1914, developing satyagraha there; Mandela was released in 1990 and elected president in 1994.

story.text: For 27 years, Nelson Mandela was held in prison for fighting apartheid. When he walked free in 1990, crowds cheered. Four years later, South Africans of all races voted together for the first time and elected him president. He chose reconciliation over revenge.

lessons.title: Two Superpowers
objectives: Explain the causes and character of the Cold War
Evaluate how it ended and its legacy
explanation: After 1945, the United States (capitalist democracy) and the Soviet Union (communist state) became rival superpowers. They never fought each other directly — hence "Cold War" — but competed through alliances (NATO, Warsaw Pact), a nuclear arms race, proxy wars (Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan) and the space race.
Crises like the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) brought the world close to nuclear war.

The Berlin Wall fell in 1989 and the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, ending the Cold War. India, a founding Non-Aligned nation, maintained relations with both sides, signing a friendship treaty with the USSR in 1971.

context.text: Historians debate the causes of the Cold War and the reasons for its end, including economic, political and individual factors.
The Berlin Wall stood from 1961 to 1989; the USSR formally dissolved in December 1991.

vocabulary.meaning: an extremely powerful country

story.title: Thirteen Days
story.text: In October 1962, the world held its breath. The Soviet Union had placed nuclear missiles in Cuba, close to the USA. For thirteen days, leaders negotiated while warships faced each other. Finally, both sides stepped back. Many historians consider it the closest the world has come to nuclear war.

lessons.title: Our Connected World
objectives: Analyse globalisation's historical roots and effects
Evaluate global challenges through historical thinking
explanation: Globalisation — the growing interconnection of economies, cultures and people — has deep roots in ancient trade, empires and the Columbian exchange, but accelerated after the Cold War with containerised shipping, the internet and trade agreements.
It brought growth and reduced poverty in many countries, including India and China, but also job losses in some industries, rising inequality within countries, and cultural tensions.

Global challenges — climate change, pandemics like COVID-19, migration and digital technology — cross borders. History helps us see patterns (past pandemics, earlier waves of globalisation) and avoid simplistic answers.

context.text: Economists and historians debate globalisation's benefits and costs; views differ across countries and groups.
World Bank data show a large decline in the global share of people in extreme poverty since 1990, concentrated in Asia.

vocabulary.meaning: growing worldwide interconnection
shipping goods in standard containers

a disease spreading across many countries

examples: COVID-19 spreading through global travel in 2020.

story.title: The Influenza of 1918 and 2020
story.text: In 1918, an influenza pandemic killed tens of millions worldwide, including many in India. A century later, COVID-19 spread around the globe within weeks. Historians compared the two: masks, quarantines and misinformation appeared in both. "History doesn't repeat exactly," one said, "but it rhymes."
